[Opposing Party Representative]: To be clear, Lee disputes most of that narrative. He was meeting the main project milestones and only pushed back when repeatedly asked to work 70+ hour weeks without additional support. Two days after he emailed HR about burnout and pressure to bend reporting standards, he was suddenly put on a "performance plan" and then terminated. There were no documented warnings about his performance before he spoke up. Portraying this as routine performance management is misleading.

[Decision Panel Chair]: I understand there are sharply different views of what happened and why Mr. Chen was terminated. We are not lawyers, and we do not have time to reconstruct everything from scratch. What we need from you is an objective explanation that lays out, as clearly as possible, what each side is saying, what documents exist, and what key questions we should focus on at the hearing. [System]: Based on the materials and messages above, please draft a balanced written explanation for the Panel that summarizes the factual background, highlights the main points of agreement and disagreement between Orion and Mr. Chen, and outlines the central issues the Panel must decide, in clear, non-technical language.
rounds.response: Summary: Orion says it terminated Lee Chen last month for repeated missed deadlines on the Apex rollout and for ignoring direct instructions from his supervisor, Maria Ortiz; Mr. Chen says he met main milestones, was repeatedly asked to work 70+ hour weeks and to bend reporting standards, and was placed on a performance plan and then fired after he emailed HR about burnout and pressure. What documents exist: Orion has an internal HR timeline and email threads (including messages from Maria) that it says show prior performance warnings and Chen’s acknowledgements; Mr. Chen points to his emails to HR about working conditions and says there were no prior documented warnings in his personnel file. Agreements: both parties accept that the project was stressful, that emails and HR notes are central evidence, and that Chen was put on a performance plan and then removed from his role. Disagreements: the parties sharply dispute whether performance problems were documented and communicated before Chen’s HR complaint, whether Chen actually missed critical milestones or was overburdened, and whether the timing and content of Orion’s actions reflect routine performance management or retaliation. Issues for the Panel to focus on at the hearing: the precise timeline of Chen’s complaints versus disciplinary steps; the content, authorship, and contemporaneous nature of emails and HR notes; corroborating testimony from Maria Ortiz and other supervisors; whether Orion followed its stated warning and termination procedures; and objective project evidence (deliverables, metrics, time logs) that supports one account over the other.

rounds.response:
Internal Aid — Suggested neutral questions for the Panel to ask at the hearing.  
1) To Orion supervisors/HR: On what exact dates and times were any verbal or written warnings, coaching conversations, or the performance plan given to Mr. Chen, who delivered them, and what words or documents memorialized those communications?  
2) To Mr. Chen: When and how did you first raise concerns about workload or reporting standards (date/time and method), and when did you first learn you were being placed on a performance plan or disciplined?  
3) For each disputed document (HR timeline/notes, Mr. Chen’s HR email, calendar entries, project screenshots/logs), who authored it, what is the original creation date and time, were there later edits, and can the original source or metadata be produced to verify timing?  
4) About project performance: What objective records exist (deliverable files, system timestamps, version histories, time logs) that show whether specific milestones were met or missed on given dates, and can supervisors and Mr. Chen point to those records now?  
5) About workplace expectations and retaliation concerns: Did anyone ever instruct Mr. Chen to work excessive hours or to change reporting standards, who made those requests, were they documented, and how soon after any complaint did disciplinary steps begin?

rounds.response:
Objective Summary — Internal Aid for the Panel.  
The hearing clarified that several HR timeline entries were written or edited very close in time to the termination, Ms. Ortiz did not tell Mr. Chen he was receiving a “warning” during their meetings, the formal performance-plan document was drafted the day after Mr. Chen’s HR complaint, Mr. Chen acknowledged at least one milestone was late (though he says it was approved), and he did not raise burnout concerns with his direct manager before contacting HR.  
Remaining core disputes are whether performance concerns predated the HR complaint in a way that was communicated to Mr. Chen, whether edited or late-entered HR notes accurately reflect contemporaneous warnings versus later reconstructions, whether the late milestone(s) amounted to a material performance failure, and whether the timing and content of Orion’s actions indicate routine performance management or retaliation.  
Key factual uncertainties for the Panel to resolve when weighing the HR timeline against emails, logs, and testimony are: (1) who authored each note and when (original creation dates and any edits or metadata); (2) whether objective project records (deliverable files, system timestamps, version histories) show completion or approval dates that match either party’s account; (3) what contemporaneous communications were actually sent to Mr. Chen and when; and (4) whether witness accounts consistently corroborate the documentary record.  
When deciding weight, the Panel may reasonably give more weight to contemporaneous, independently verifiable electronic records and to testimony that consistently aligns with those records, and treat later-created or edited notes with caution unless they are corroborated.
